The Water Down Stream

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A billion rand has been spent on cleaning up the Hartbeespoort dam, but why are we fixing the symptom and not the problem?

Unique Selling Point:
We are going to follow both the hennops river and jukskei river, where they join to become the crocodile river and into the Hartbeespoort dam. This river system supports Pretoria, and the entire NorthWest province. We will track the eColi count at several strategic positions and then see if the waste water treatment facilities are working properly. We already know they are over capacity, and the Department of Water Affairs admitted they had not even done the green drop report since 2014, and had UNDERspent by 2 billion rand! We have made a google map to show the different locations - we will interview case studies along the river and the department of north west water affairs regarding how Gauteng exports the problem downstream. The evidence we have already collected is good and shows that our water is in a dire condition.

Summary:
4.2 billion litre's of untreated waste water runs into our rivers everyday. Two years ago, the water in the Hennops was so bad that Afriforum laid criminal charges against Ekhuruleni municipality as there were around 50 leaking sewage pipes from Tembisa township alone. The sewage treatment facilities (Sunderland and Olifantsfontein) are both over capacity according to the last known water drop reports in 2014... who knows what it is 4 years later (it would have been tested in 2013). We went back and the river water is marginally better (awaiting tests), but the problem in Hartbeespoort is still very bad. Ivory park which is across the river from Tembisa falls under the city of johannesburg, and there we met a couple whose garden and home was literally on a broken sewage pipe that often leaks into their house. We interviewed them, and while doing the interview, the pipe across the street began as well. Is it that only on threat of legal action that these municipalities act? Julius Kleynhans who was at Afriforum, and now works at OUTA is considering building another case against the city of johannesburg. The case will be retrospective and he suggests we widen our story to incorporate the Jukskei river because when that meets up with the Hennops, together they form the crocodile river, which flows into Hartbeespoort. We would test the water by Alexandra, by the leaking sewage pipes by dainfern/steyn city and after the Northern sewage works, at the crocodile river, and in the dam near the water's abstraction point. Sewage water carries bacteria and disease causing bacteria and there have been several warnings in the Harties area regarding the use of their taps.

Further information:
We visited Leriba lodge on the water's edge and met with the owner Pieter Du Preez, whose river banks on the estate are covered in trash. He has trained his staff in the art of botany and they are using the plants to keep the soil from eroding, and they do weekly cleanups - all which we filmed. While there we saw several people living along the rivers edge - using the water to wash their clothes and cook food. The problem is, that if you don't have access to taps, rivers are still a major source of water for millions of people in South Africa.

Extra Budget Items:
Research to go and test the water along the Hennops and Jukskei rivers with Julius. And we will need to go to Harties and speak to the locals to find case studies of how bad the water has been. (3 days)
Pay Abram Rapelwana to go and video of Diepsloot overflowing

Press Release:


Dirty Rivers
Over the years, hundreds of millions of rands have been spent to try and clean up the Hartbeespoort dam, which is infested with deadly bacteria and e-coli from sewage spills. But it seems government has largely ignored the source of the problem. Carte Blanche follows the Hennops, Jukskei and Crocodile rivers to witness the shocking state of Gauteng and North-West Provinces’ water sources first-hand.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Bongani Bingwa


Script:


In February this year, the Hartbeespoort dam was pot-marked by water hyacinth… Warnings that this would get worse were ignored, and last week, the green suffocating mass had taken over. THAT same water is abstracted to be used as drinking water for residents along the shoreline … which now looks like THIS. Residents say if they drink it, they get diarrhoea.
Andries: “I got an allergic reaction on my skin. It was really bad. It’s not nice to shower in water like that.”
LINK: “I’m standing at Hartbeespoort Dam. Water flows into here from the crocodile river, and it’s laced with nutrient, which carries faecal matter, and that’s why this hyacinth has grown almost as far as the eye can see. Now
To my right, is the sewage pump which is more than 40 years old, but residents tell us that last month it didn’t work for straight 25 days before the municipality fixed it. And immediately, ahead of me, about 150m is the abstraction point which carried water for about 24,000 people in the area.”
Dr. Botha: “A lot of the water that goes into the catchment of the dam, comes through the kidneys of the millions of inhabitants living in this area.”
Environmental scientist Dr. Frikkie Botha calculated that 349 tonnes of nutrient from phosphates are arriving here every year, which is why 30% of the dam is covered in water Hyacinth. Underneath that, lying dormant, is Blue Green algae, which produces a deadly neurotoxin.
Frikkie: “Which must be treated in a small waste water treatment plant that was designed for normal water, NOT for this eutrophide system.”
Link: “This is the abstraction point for the Hartbeespoort dam. And the Hyacinth is here, because the water is contaminated. This is what comes out, and that’s why residents in the area have had to resort to expensive filtration systems.”
Andries Lombaard, chair of the Hartbeespoort inhabitants forum, which falls within the jurisdiction of the Madibeng Municipality, says a home filtration system is a necessity.
Andries: “This is about R70,000, you had to do it, because otherwise you couldn’t drink the water.”
The National Department of Water and Sanitation is the regulator of our drinking water quality around the country. Sputnik Ratau, is its spokesperson.
Sputnik: “We have some work to do around Madibeng. The issues of water do not know any level of government. We are ultimately the custodians of our water resources whether it be potable or waste water.”
Madibeng Municipality, in a written response, accepts that the dam is “highly eutrophic”, but says that its tap water from the dam is of an acceptable “drinking standard”. However, as long ago as 2013, a report conducted with the municipality, said the water exceeded South African National Standard limits. And then last year, a second report conducted with Tshwane University of Technology, concluded that the water was contaminated.
Dr. Botha: “We could prove, that under the conditions of an algae bloom there are traces of microcysthys in the drinking water, there are studies that indicate that this kind of toxin could be the starting point of cancerous situation in the liver.”
Water scientist Julius Kleynhans, the water portfolio director for OUTA, says spending money on cleaning the dam is futile.
Julius Kleynhans: “They’ve chucked in millions of rands, we know about 240 million rand has been spent in 2012, and they’ve also budgeted almost a billion rand, it’s treating the symptoms and not the cause.”
So we investigated upstream and tested the Hennops, Jukskei, and Crocodile rivers with Julius Kleynhans. We began with the Hennops, which runs through Tembisa township.
Julius: “It showed that it’s raw sewage. It means there were a million of ecoli per 100ml – that is over a million (shows bottle)
Bongani: “How bad is that?”
Julius: “It’s severe. You know the health implications… people will die.”
Dr. Irwin Jukes is a seasoned Microbacterial expert.
Dr. Jukes: “The Ecoli is a microorganism it’s always an indicator of sewage contamination.”
Ivory park is in Midrand, and falls under Joburg water. City bylaws are not enforced, resulting in manholes freely over-flowing through properties.
MMC for Water and Sanitation at Joburg City, Nico de Jager, says they do respond, but manholes are often blocked again 6 weeks later.
Nico de jager: “The pollution that we see in the dams, is a result of bad human behaviour.”
Nolitha: “This water stinks.”(Lamanzianukakakulu.)
Nolitha Vincy grew tired of waiting for an RDP home and built her own. A manhole in her garden overflows regularly.
Nolitha Vincy: (zulu): “Sometimes this water comes into our room, its coming inside the room.”
Across the street, another manhole begins to ooze. Etienne Hugo is general manager of operations for Joburg Water.
Etienne: “You find like lot of solid waste, you know that you find in your normal households, you find a lot of nappies, sometimes unfortunately find a lot of foetuses in the sewer infrastructure.”
Here, a running tap is a luxury, whilst carrying water home is a daily struggle. As we travel downstream, the dependency on the grey river water for cooking or washing clothes becomes more apparent.
Dr. Jukes: “Basically that’s the colour of the sewage contamination. The water will get clearer and then you’ll see lumps of stuff floating on it and, foaming tends to increase as one goes further downstream.”
Next we went to test the Jukskei river, which begins in this wetland near Bruma.
Bruma link: “Its grey green, it’s murky, and yup it smells! This water is contaminated by abandoned buildings, faulty pipes and sewage spillages.
This cloud-like foam may be mistaken for a bubble bath. But it’s actually a sewage spill. Three weeks ago, raw, untreated sewage seeped from these manholes.
To catch the spills earlier Joburg City’s new real time monitoring system searches the 12,000 kilometre maze of underground pipes for blockages.
Etienne: “We are busy with a bioremediation process to treat the water, what was contaminated due to the sewer.”
Joburg Water budgeted R10 million to upgrade their pipes.
Etienne: “The best practice is to replace about 2% of your infrastructure currently we are just below 1%.”
A month after the clean-up, and the sludgy substances and sewage fungus, which grow from nitrates and phosphates, remain.
Jukes: “Eutrophication is where you have an accumulation of nutrients, it leads to an overgrowth of microorganisms or algae that would not normally be there.”
Downstream in Alexandra, women wash clothes nearby this decommissioned water treatment facility. The ecoli levels here were in the millions.
Bongani: “Does that shock you at all?”
Sputnik: “It does shock me, in the sense that it shouldn’t be there, and that is why as a regulator, it is upon us to engage with the City that is responsible for it. One of the things we need to actually keep working on is the pollution due to human behaviour…”
Bongani: “But obviously not everything can be blamed on communities living on or near the rivers.”
Sputnik: “The authorizations that we give to the WWTW prescribe how they need to perform, where there is failure, there is action that is taken.”
Bongani: Eight years after my first engagement with this Department, I’m bringing the same issues to you?
Sputnik: But the failure is not constant. It is one issue married to others, and ultimately it is a combination of everything.”
But, when we went further downstream near Diepsloot to the Northern Works Waste Water Treatment Plant, our tests showed that some waste water is leaving the plant untreated.
Etienne: “Frequent operational failures due to aging infrastructure is what we’re sitting with at the northern works.”
Etienne Hugo says their two sewage overflow dams were never cleaned and silted up.
Etienne: “There’s currently a project to de-sludge it to remove all the sediment in the dams, and we’re lining to regulation.”
The effect of aging infrastructure is magnified by the dramatic increase in population numbers.
Etienne: “We’ve calculated you need about 1.2 billion rand, a year to take care of the existing infra now we currently have say about 60/50% of that funding.”
The city says it is planning to alleviate the pressure on the Northern Works.
MMC De Jager: “We are at the moment in talks with financial institutions to build the Lanseria WWTP to further assist the Northern waste water treatment plant.”
The situation begs the question as to whether this is not the function of the state, but the department of water and sanitation is reportedly bankrupt.
Bongani: “Is the department broke?”
Sputnik: “The department so far, as I know it, is paying those bills that are before it. We have enough money to be able to do what we need to do for the next financial year.”
Clearly, that money hasn’t extended to preventing massive sewage flows into the Jukskei river. Our tests revealed the nitrate levels, likely from urine, were 110 times over the limit, while the phosphates were a 125 times over the limit.
Julius: “There’s a lot of manholes and sewage facilities that’s dumping untreated sewage, actually raw, which is criminal, and its pouring toxic waste into our river systems.”
BUT MMC de Jager says it’s not just sewage that’s flowing into the river.
de Jager: “We need to look at reducing the phosphate footprint in our washing powders, and in our soaps etc”
The Jukskei flows past the densely populated area of Diepsloot.
Bongani link: “Perhaps the most overpowering thing about this place is the smell. My shoes are deep in a mixture of what looks like mud and faecal matter…What is amazing is that there are ppl living right here, somebody’s garden is right there, and well their water is comes from this mess.”
Tributaries of the Jukskei flow through the township, winding up in stagnant pools – filled with effluent and rubbish. This is carried into the crocodile river – which ALSO tested positive for ecoli. Outas Julius Kleynhans believes the national department is responsible for not enforcing the law.
Bongani: “So all these rivers are polluted?”
Julius: “Yes and I think this is a bigger picture of the country. I think its complete incompetence not to follow through on compliance monitoring and enforcement.”
Sputnik: “Monitoring does not imply that failure will not happen, it is meant to assist that when that failure happens in order to be able to correct that failure.”
The crocodile river flows directly into the Hartbeespoort dam. Of the 190 houses built at Refentse, an RDP settlement near the dam ONLY 30 have been connected to the sewage system. Zonke Masango has to walk through sewage daily.
Zonke Masango: “This is coming from the toilets. Eish it smells bad… its shit here... Just imagine, cooking, eating, smelling this situation.”
Madibeng in a written response acknowledged the challenges at Refentse, but promised to “ensure that such spillages are avoided.”
Zonke: “This is our reality that we are living in because of a poor settlement, we are forced to live with this thing.
Julius Kleynhans: “I believe, if one municipal manager gets locked up, it will change water management in this country severely.”

Bongani: “Does that shock you at all?” Sputnik: “It does shock me, in the sense that it shouldn’t be there, and that is why as a regulator, it is upon us to engage with the City that is responsible for it. One of the things we need to actually keep working on is the pollution due to human behaviour…” Bongani: “But obviously not everything can be blamed on communities living on or near the rivers.” Sputnik: “The authorizations that we give to the WWTW prescribe how they need to perform, where there is failure, there is action that is taken.” Bongani: Eight years after my first engagement with this Department, I’m bringing the same issues to you? Sputnik: But the failure is not constant. It is one issue married to others, and ultimately it is a combination of everything.” But, when we went further downstream near Diepsloot to the Northern Works Waste Water Treatment Plant, our tests showed that some waste water is leaving the plant untreated. Etienne: “Frequent operational failures due to aging infrastructure is what we’re sitting with at the northern works.” Etienne Hugo says their two sewage overflow dams were never cleaned and silted up. Etienne: “There’s currently a project to de-sludge it to remove all the sediment in the dams, and we’re lining to regulation.” The effect of aging infrastructure is magnified by the dramatic increase in population numbers. Etienne: “We’ve calculated you need about 1.2 billion rand, a year to take care of the existing infra now we currently have say about 60/50% of that funding.” The city says it is planning to alleviate the pressure on the Northern Works. MMC De Jager: “We are at the moment in talks with financial institutions to build the Lanseria WWTP to further assist the Northern waste water treatment plant.” The situation begs the question as to whether this is not the function of the state, but the department of water and sanitation is reportedly bankrupt. Bongani: “Is the department broke?” Sputnik: “The department so far, as I know it, is paying those bills that are before it. We have enough money to be able to do what we need to do for the next financial year.” Clearly, that money hasn’t extended to preventing massive sewage flows into the Jukskei river. Our tests revealed the nitrate levels, likely from urine, were 110 times over the limit, while the phosphates were a 125 times over the limit. Julius: “There’s a lot of manholes and sewage facilities that’s dumping untreated sewage, actually raw, which is criminal, and its pouring toxic waste into our river systems.” BUT MMC de Jager says it’s not just sewage that’s flowing into the river. de Jager: “We need to look at reducing the phosphate footprint in our washing powders, and in our soaps etc” The Jukskei flows past the densely populated area of Diepsloot. Bongani link: “Perhaps the most overpowering thing about this place is the smell. My shoes are deep in a mixture of what looks like mud and faecal matter…What is amazing is that there are ppl living right here, somebody’s garden is right there, and well their water is comes from this mess.” Tributaries of the Jukskei flow through the township, winding up in stagnant pools – filled with effluent and rubbish. This is carried into the crocodile river – which ALSO tested positive for ecoli. Outas Julius Kleynhans believes the national department is responsible for not enforcing the law. Bongani: “So all these rivers are polluted?” Julius: “Yes and I think this is a bigger picture of the country. I think its complete incompetence not to follow through on compliance monitoring and enforcement.” Sputnik: “Monitoring does not imply that failure will not happen, it is meant to assist that when that failure happens in order to be able to correct that failure.” The crocodile river flows directly into the Hartbeespoort dam. Of the 190 houses built at Refentse, an RDP settlement near the dam ONLY 30 have been connected to the sewage system. Zonke Masango has to walk through sewage daily. Zonke Masango: “This is coming from the toilets. Eish it smells bad… its shit here... Just imagine, cooking, eating, smelling this situation.” Madibeng in a written response acknowledged the challenges at Refentse, but promised to “ensure that such spillages are avoided.” Zonke: “This is our reality that we are living in because of a poor settlement, we are forced to live with this thing. Julius Kleynhans: “I believe, if one municipal manager gets locked up, it will change water management in this country severely.”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A billion rand has been spent on cleaning up the Hartbeespoort dam, but why are we fixing the symptom and not the problem?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We are going to follow both the hennops river and jukskei river, where they join to become the crocodile river and into the Hartbeespoort dam. This river system supports Pretoria, and the entire NorthWest province. We will track the eColi count at several strategic positions and then see if the waste water treatment facilities are working properly. We already know they are over capacity, and the Department of Water Affairs admitted they had not even done the green drop report since 2014, and had UNDERspent by 2 billion rand! We have made a google map to show the different locations - we will interview case studies along the river and the department of north west water affairs regarding how Gauteng exports the problem downstream. The evidence we have already collected is good and shows that our water is in a dire condition.
metadata.Summary: 4.2 billion litre's of untreated waste water runs into our rivers everyday. Two years ago, the water in the Hennops was so bad that Afriforum laid criminal charges against Ekhuruleni municipality as there were around 50 leaking sewage pipes from Tembisa township alone. The sewage treatment facilities (Sunderland and Olifantsfontein) are both over capacity according to the last known water drop reports in 2014... who knows what it is 4 years later (it would have been tested in 2013). We went back and the river water is marginally better (awaiting tests), but the problem in Hartbeespoort is still very bad. Ivory park which is across the river from Tembisa falls under the city of johannesburg, and there we met a couple whose garden and home was literally on a broken sewage pipe that often leaks into their house. We interviewed them, and while doing the interview, the pipe across the street began as well. Is it that only on threat of legal action that these municipalities act? Julius Kleynhans who was at Afriforum, and now works at OUTA is considering building another case against the city of johannesburg. The case will be retrospective and he suggests we widen our story to incorporate the Jukskei river because when that meets up with the Hennops, together they form the crocodile river, which flows into Hartbeespoort. We would test the water by Alexandra, by the leaking sewage pipes by dainfern/steyn city and after the Northern sewage works, at the crocodile river, and in the dam near the water's abstraction point. Sewage water carries bacteria and disease causing bacteria and there have been several warnings in the Harties area regarding the use of their taps.
metadata.Further information: We visited Leriba lodge on the water's edge and met with the owner Pieter Du Preez, whose river banks on the estate are covered in trash. He has trained his staff in the art of botany and they are using the plants to keep the soil from eroding, and they do weekly cleanups - all which we filmed. While there we saw several people living along the rivers edge - using the water to wash their clothes and cook food. The problem is, that if you don't have access to taps, rivers are still a major source of water for millions of people in South Africa.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: Research to go and test the water along the Hennops and Jukskei rivers with Julius. And we will need to go to Harties and speak to the locals to find case studies of how bad the water has been. (3 days) Pay Abram Rapelwana to go and video of Diepsloot overflowing
